title: The Overtime Multiplier: Why an Extra Trading Hour Before Christmas Rarely Pays for Itself
linkedin:
Christmas rosters are getting locked in across the East Coast right now, and the assumption behind most of them is simple: more trading hours means more revenue means more profit.

The middle step gets skipped. More revenue is not automatically more profit, because the hour you add rarely costs what the hours already on the roster cost.

Here is the arithmetic worth running before the shift goes live. On a 40 percent gross margin, an hour that brings in $400 in extra sales contributes $160 in gross profit before labour is counted. Staff that hour at a normal loaded wage cost of $55 and it still clears $105.

Move the same hour onto a public holiday, where the loaded cost might run closer to $90 once penalty rates and superannuation are counted, and the contribution nearly halves. Run a leaner 25 percent margin through the same shift and it can tip into contributing almost nothing, even with the till ringing all afternoon.

The pattern we see across owner-led retail and hospitality businesses heading into Christmas is that the roster gets filled on instinct, extra Sundays, longer evenings, another casual on the floor, with the contribution of each hour worked out in January rather than before the shift is booked.

Not every extra hour is a mistake. Hours that create genuinely new demand, rather than just moving the same customers to a different time of day, are worth the loaded cost. The distinction only becomes visible once the calculation is actually run.

Locking in your Christmas trading hours this week? Quick gut check before the roster goes out.

An extra hour open does not cost the same as your regular hours. Penalty rates, casual loading and super can add up fast, especially on evenings, weekends and public holidays like Boxing Day.

Run the numbers on a typical hour and it still stacks up fine. Run them on a public holiday shift with a thinner margin and some hours barely break even, even while the till is busy all afternoon.

The question worth asking before the extra shift is booked: is this hour bringing in new customers, or just moving the same ones to a different time of day?

Has anyone actually checked whether your Christmas roster is making money, or just revenue?

A practical note for retail, hospitality and trade business owners across Brisbane, Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria as Christmas rosters are being finalised this week.

Extending trading hours over the festive season feels like a straightforward way to capture extra sales, but the extra hour rarely costs the same as hours already on the roster. Evening, weekend and public holiday loadings, plus casual on-costs, can lift the wage cost of a shift well above the standard rate, sometimes close to double on a day such as Boxing Day. Weighed against the actual gross profit the hour brings in, some extended shifts barely break even, even when trade looks busy.

The useful exercise, and it only takes an afternoon, is to compare the realistic extra revenue from a shift against its full loaded wage cost before the roster is locked in. Hours that bring in genuinely new customers are usually worth running. Hours that simply move existing customers to a different time of day add cost without adding sales.

Worth working through before December, rather than finding out the answer once the quarter's results are in. Read the full piece on the ProfitPulse blog.
